turns.prompt_text: I have a fish feeder idea where I use one of those 5 gallon water jugs and fill it with fish food, this tank of fish food then supplies some sort of shooter mechanism that will shoot the fish food into the pond. Between that, there is some kind of a auger release mechanism that will allow food out of the tank and into the shooting chamber. I have a few thoughts about this. The main problem I see is that this 5 gallon fish food tank will be heavy, if I have the auger releasing food downward so that is going with gravity. The problem is that I will need some very sturdy stand to hold this over time, I would most likely just use 2x4s then. This problem is pretty well solved. The other solution I have would be to just leave it alone and leave it on the ground but use some kind of double auger for variable to pull the fish food up. I feel like I might need to explore this route cuz there's something I might need here. I'm also thinking that the energy required to pull the fish food up might be significantly more than the order that just releases the food down, but I'm not really sure because the one that releases down still kind of grinds against the walls. My main reason for wanting to raise the fish food up is so that it can go down some tubes or slides for movement I could essentially use a vertical auger, but I think slanting it like a conveyor would be easier
turns.response_html:
Your instincts about exploring the ground-based, upward-pulling method are spot on. While it seems like lifting the food against gravity would require more energy, the slanted auger actually solves a major mechanical problem called head pressure.

If you place a 5-gallon jug directly over a downward auger, the entire weight of that food presses down on the mechanism. This packs the pellets tightly, creating friction that often crushes the food into dust, jams the blades, and stalls the motor.

By leaving the heavy tank on the ground and using a slanted tube to pull the food up (essentially an Archimedes screw), you separate the bulk weight of the 5-gallon supply from the lifting mechanism. The motor only has to do the work of lifting the small amount of food currently inside the tube.

Here is how to approach the slanted conveyor build:

1. The Sweet Spot Angle

A vertical auger requires the food to be perfectly cupped by the blade, which often causes pellets to fall backward (rollback). Slanting the auger like a conveyor at roughly a 30 to 45-degree angle is the most efficient configuration. It creates a natural bucket effect within the tube, lifting the pellets smoothly without needing a massive motor, while still gaining enough height to drop the food down a slide into your shooter chamber.

2. Tube and Pellet Clearance

The biggest cause of failure in DIY feeders is the gap between the auger blade (the "flighting") and the inner wall of the tube. If the gap is exactly the size of a fish food pellet, pellets will get wedged in the gap and act like brake pads, halting the motor.

  • The solution: Ensure the gap is either significantly smaller than a single pellet (so they can't get trapped) or comfortably larger (so they slide freely).

3. Fabricating the Components

Standard PVC piping makes an excellent housing for the slanted conveyor. For the complex internal geometry, you can 3D print the internal auger flights in modular sections and slide them over a central metal drive rod. You can also print custom housing connectors—like a tapered Y-junction funnel—to smoothly transition the food from the mouth of the 5-gallon jug directly into the base of the PVC tube.

For the structural support, a simple wooden cradle or A-frame built from scrap 2x4s will easily hold the slanted PVC pipe and the attached motor steady on the ground.

turns.prompt_text: So the main purpose of this is to act as a gate, I imagine this Archimedes screw is better than just a basic conveyor belt with like u-shaped teeth, and I really don't want it to go that far cuz I want the shooter relatively close to it, he could
turns.response_html:
Your intuition is completely right—avoiding a belt conveyor with U-teeth for this is a smart move. Belts with paddle teeth are prone to jamming if a stray pellet wedges between the tooth and the housing wall, and they take up way too much linear footprint when you want everything compact.

An Archimedes screw (or tubular auger) is ideal here precisely because it functions simultaneously as a conveying mechanism and a positive gate.

By using the auger to lift the food a short distance from a ground-level intake up into your shooter chamber, you get two major mechanical advantages:

1. Built-In Metering (The Gate Function)

Unlike a gravity drop where food can potentially free-flow or slip past when you don't want it to, a closed-tube auger acts as a strict volumetric gate. Every single rotation of the screw moves a fixed, predictable pocket of fish food forward.

  • When the motor is off, the solid columns of pellets trapped between the flighting and the tube act as a physical block, stopping any food from trickling down or spilling into the shooter.
  • When the motor on, it meters out exact amounts. You can precisely control your feeding portions simply by counting motor rotations or timing how long it spins.

2. Keeping the Footprint Tight

Because you want the shooter close to the supply without building a massive tower of 2x4s, a short, steeply inclined PVC auger (housed right alongside or beneath the 5-gallon jug) keeps the physical footprint minimal. The 5-gallon jug can sit low and stable on the ground, a short curved tube or printed funnel feeds the intake zone at the bottom, and the auger punches the food up just high enough to clear the lip of your shooting chamber.
